title: Expressing Purpose: To, For and So That
summary: Express why people do things and what objects are for. Contrast a purpose infinitive with for + noun and for + -ing, attach infinitives to nouns such as a place or someone, and express intended results with so that + a modal verb.
learningObjectives: Explain a reason for an action using to + base verb, including the purpose of a person, action or object.
Use noun + to-infinitive expressions and keep needed final prepositions in phrases such as a seat to sit on.
Choose for + noun, for someone to do something and for + -ing correctly when describing people, purposes and functions.
State intended outcomes and prevention with so that + can/could/will/would, including negative forms and omission of that.

explanation.heading: Use to + infinitive to explain why an action happens
explanation.body: An infinitive with to can tell us the purpose of an action or explain why something exists or is needed. Use to + base verb after the main action: visited the office to collect a form. It usually answers “why?” rather than describing an earlier completed result. Do not replace this purpose infinitive with for + -ing to describe a person’s reason for taking an action.
explanation.example: We walked to the other building to collect the spare equipment.

explanation.heading: Attach a useful infinitive to a noun
explanation.body: An infinitive can specify what someone can or needs to do with a thing, person or opportunity: something to read, work to finish, someone to consult, time to prepare. When the verb requires a preposition, keep it at the end: a desk to work at, a colleague to talk to, or a tool to open a can with.
explanation.example: Could you find me a quiet place to work in during the call?

explanation.heading: Distinguish for + noun from to + verb
explanation.body: Use for before a noun phrase that names the aim or intended recipient: stopped for refreshments. Use to + base verb when you name the intended action: stopped to buy refreshments. The longer form for + someone + to + verb states who will carry out the action, often with a different subject: I left the instructions for Ava to follow.
explanation.example: We reserved a front-row seat for the interpreter to use.

explanation.heading: Describe the function of an object with for + -ing
explanation.body: Use be for + -ing to identify what an object is designed or commonly used for: this clip is for holding papers together. A purpose infinitive often describes the reason a person chose an action: I bought the clip to organise my documents. This contrast separates an object’s function from a person’s reason for acting. Ask “What is this for?” to find out an object’s purpose.
explanation.example: These soft pads are for protecting the floor beneath the furniture.

explanation.heading: Show intended results with so that
explanation.body: Use so that + a clause when you describe a result someone wants to make possible or prevent. It commonly takes can/could for ability and will/would for expected outcomes, with past forms when appropriate. Negative modal forms help describe prevention: so that nobody could see the screen. The word that can often be left out without changing the meaning.
explanation.example: We shared the agenda early so that everyone could prepare questions.

comparisons.title: A noun goal versus an action goal

left.label: For + noun
left.example: They stopped for a short break.
left.note: For introduces the break as a noun phrase naming the purpose.

right.label: To + verb
right.example: They stopped to rest for ten minutes.
right.note: To rest names the action they intended to take.

comparisons.title: A personal reason versus an intended outcome

left.label: To + verb
left.example: I moved closer to hear the announcement.
left.note: The infinitive explains why the person moved.

right.label: So that + clause
right.example: I moved closer so that I could hear the announcement.
right.note: The subordinate clause describes the intended result using could.

examples.sentence: I opened the window to let some fresh air into the room.
examples.note: The infinitive explains why the speaker opened the window.

examples.sentence: There is a high shelf to store the spare cables on.
examples.note: The final on is necessary because we store things on a shelf.

examples.sentence: The organiser set aside a microphone for the guest speaker to use.
examples.note: For + the guest speaker + to use identifies who will use the object.

examples.sentence: This waterproof pouch is for keeping papers dry.
examples.note: For + -ing describes the object’s intended function.

examples.sentence: We checked the timetable twice so we would not miss the last train.
examples.note: So without that can express a negative intended outcome using would not.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I went upstairs for collect my jacket.
commonMistakes.correct: I went upstairs to collect my jacket.
commonMistakes.why: A person’s reason for doing something takes a purpose infinitive to + verb.

commonMistakes.incorrect: There was no chair to sit, so I stood throughout the talk.
commonMistakes.correct: There was no chair to sit on, so I stood throughout the talk.
commonMistakes.why: Sit on requires on when the noun being modified is a chair.

commonMistakes.incorrect: These gloves are for protect your hands from the cold.
commonMistakes.correct: These gloves are for protecting your hands from the cold.
commonMistakes.why: For + -ing explains what the gloves are used for.

commonMistakes.incorrect: He dimmed the lights so that the audience could saw the screen.
commonMistakes.correct: He dimmed the lights so that the audience could see the screen.
commonMistakes.why: A modal such as could takes a base verb, here see rather than saw.

studyTips: When the goal follows a main action, ask whether you are naming a noun (for supplies) or an action (to buy supplies).
Practice noun + infinitive phrases, checking whether the main verb needs a trailing preposition: a tool to cut with, a seat to sit on.
Rewrite a purpose infinitive as so that + could/would, then make a negative version to explain what someone wanted to avoid.

exercises.prompt: After the alarm sounded, staff opened the side door ___ everyone leave quickly.
exercises.feedback: To help explains why the staff opened the door; for helping does not describe the purpose of their action.

exercises.prompt: The hikers stopped at the village shop ___ more drinking water.
exercises.feedback: To buy states the intended action that motivated the stop.

exercises.prompt: This reusable sleeve is ___ documents dry during the journey.
exercises.feedback: For keeping identifies what the sleeve is designed to do; a preposition takes the -ing form.

exercises.prompt: The instructor repeated the demonstration so that everyone ___ follow each step.
exercises.feedback: So that + could + base verb describes the intended result in the past.

exercises.prompt: I returned to the studio ___ before the building closed. (collect my notebook; use to + infinitive)
acceptedAnswers: to collect my notebook
exercises.feedback: To collect my notebook explains the speaker’s reason for returning.

exercises.prompt: They carried extra water ___ during the long walk. (the hikers / drink; use for + person + to-infinitive)
acceptedAnswers: for the hikers to drink
exercises.feedback: For the hikers to drink specifies who was intended to use the water.

exercises.prompt: Is there a quiet corner ___ while I wait? (sit / in; use to + verb + final preposition, without adding a subject)
acceptedAnswers: to sit in
exercises.feedback: The infinitive to sit requires in because the speaker sits in a corner.

exercises.prompt: I saved the address yesterday ___ it again today. (so that / I / would not have to / search for)
acceptedAnswers: so that I wouldn't have to search for
so that I would not have to search for
exercises.feedback: So that I would not have to describes the result the speaker intended; the auxiliary would is followed by the base form have.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the purpose expression: We met early for discuss the results.
acceptedAnswers: We met early to discuss the results.
exercises.feedback: Use to discuss, not for discuss, for the reason people met.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the verb form after for: This thick cloth is for clean the camera lens.
acceptedAnswers: This thick cloth is for cleaning the camera lens.
exercises.feedback: For cleaning identifies the function of the cloth and requires -ing.

exercises.prompt: Correct the missing preposition: There was not a bench to sit, so we stood.
acceptedAnswers: There was not a bench to sit on, so we stood.
exercises.feedback: A bench is something to sit on; the preposition remains at the end of the infinitive phrase.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the verb form after could: I wrote the instructions clearly so that the trainees could understood them.
acceptedAnswers: I wrote the instructions clearly so that the trainees could understand them.
exercises.feedback: Could is followed by the base verb understand, not the past form understood.

speakingExercises.prompt: You phoned the caretaker because you wanted a spare key. Begin with “I phoned the caretaker” and use to + “ask for a spare key”.
acceptedAnswers: I phoned the caretaker to ask for a spare key.
speakingExercises.feedback: To ask describes the purpose of the call.

speakingExercises.prompt: What is this label used for? It identifies luggage. Begin with “The label is for” and use the -ing form of identify.
acceptedAnswers: The label is for identifying luggage.
speakingExercises.feedback: For identifying describes the label’s function.

speakingExercises.prompt: Report the group’s short stop using the exact information: we / stop / for a snack / yesterday. Use the past simple and for + noun.
acceptedAnswers: We stopped for a snack yesterday.
speakingExercises.feedback: For a snack names the purpose as a noun phrase.

speakingExercises.prompt: A visitor needs a place to rest. Say exactly one sentence starting “There is a bench” and ending “on”, using a to-infinitive with sit.
acceptedAnswers: There is a bench to sit on.
There's a bench to sit on.
speakingExercises.feedback: To sit on correctly retains the preposition that connects sitting to the bench.

speakingExercises.prompt: Yesterday you brought extra markers because you wanted everyone to be able to draw. Start with “I brought extra markers” and use so that everyone could.
acceptedAnswers: I brought extra markers so that everyone could draw.
speakingExercises.feedback: So that + everyone could expresses the intended result.

speakingExercises.prompt: You left a note because Lina needed to read it. Say one sentence beginning with “I left” and use “a note for Lina to read”.
acceptedAnswers: I left a note for Lina to read.
speakingExercises.feedback: For Lina to read states who is expected to perform the action.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences. First, begin “I bought a brush” and explain its purpose with “to clean the keyboard”. Second, begin “The brush is for” and give its function using “removing dust”.
acceptedAnswers: I bought a brush to clean the keyboard. The brush is for removing dust.
speakingExercises.feedback: The first sentence gives a person’s purpose; the second gives the object’s function.

speakingExercises.prompt: During yesterday’s meeting, he muted his phone to prevent interruptions. Begin with “He muted his phone” and finish using “so that it would not interrupt the meeting”.
acceptedAnswers: He muted his phone so that it would not interrupt the meeting.
He muted his phone so that it wouldn't interrupt the meeting.
speakingExercises.feedback: So that it would not + base verb names the unwanted outcome being prevented.

listeningExercises.audioText: I hurried to the library to return a borrowed atlas before the doors closed.
listeningExercises.prompt: Why did the speaker rush to the library?
listeningExercises.feedback: To return identifies the purpose of rushing to the library.

listeningExercises.audioText: The soft cloth in this kit is for polishing glass, not for drying dishes.
listeningExercises.prompt: What is the cleaning cloth designed to do?
listeningExercises.feedback: For polishing glass describes its intended use, not the other activities.

listeningExercises.audioText: I left a spare charger for Jamal to use during the trip.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the four-word phrase immediately after “charger”.
acceptedAnswers: for Jamal to use
listeningExercises.feedback: For Jamal to use names the intended user of the charger.

listeningExercises.audioText: They arranged a video call so that their cousins overseas could join the celebration.
listeningExercises.prompt: What did the video call make possible?
listeningExercises.feedback: So that their cousins could join makes the intended result explicit.

listeningExercises.audioText: There is a sturdy stool to stand on if you cannot reach the top shelf.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker suggest using to reach a high shelf?
listeningExercises.feedback: A low stool to stand on is the object made available for reaching the shelf.

listeningExercises.audioText: Before the presentation, Nadia dimmed the lights so the screen would be easier to see.
listeningExercises.prompt: Why did Nadia dim the lights?
choices: To make the screen easier to see.
listeningExercises.feedback: The intended consequence was better visibility of the screen.

listeningExercises.audioText: I packed a sandwich to eat between the morning classes.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two words immediately after “sandwich”.
acceptedAnswers: to eat
listeningExercises.feedback: To eat introduces the intended purpose of packing the sandwich.

listeningExercises.audioText: The padded strap is for carrying the bag over your shoulder.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word phrase immediately after “for”.
acceptedAnswers: carrying the bag
listeningExercises.feedback: For carrying the bag expresses the purpose for which the strap is designed.
